import { Callout, Code, CodeBlock, H2, Prose } from "../../components/content"; import { MathBlock } from "../../components/content/Math.jsx"; const content = { title: "Exponential Families & Sufficient Statistics", readTime: "~38 min", content: () =>

1. Why this pattern keeps appearing in machine learning

Bernoulli classification, softmax class probabilities, Poisson event counts, Gaussian regression, and many Bayesian updates look different on the surface. Exponential families reveal a shared structure underneath. That structure gives us compact likelihoods, stable optimisation, interpretable links in generalised linear models, and convenient conjugate priors. The point is not to memorise a formula. It is to recognise when a model can reduce a dataset to the information relevant for its parameters, and why the resulting objective has such friendly gradients.

2. The exponential-family form

A distribution belongs to the exponential family if it can be written in the form below. The natural parameter eta controls the distribution, the sufficient statistic T(x) extracts information from one observation, the base measure h(x) handles terms unrelated to eta, and the log-partition function A(eta) makes the density normalise correctly. {`p(x|\\eta)=h(x)\\exp\\left(\\eta^\\mathsf{T}T(x)-A(\\eta)\\right)`} The name can feel intimidating because of the exponential, but the form is mostly useful bookkeeping: it separates data-dependent terms from parameter-dependent terms. For independent observations, the joint log-likelihood depends on the dataset through a sum of statistics. {`\\log p(x_{1:n}|\\eta)=\\eta^\\mathsf{T}\\sum_{i=1}^{n}T(x_i)-nA(\\eta)+\\text{terms independent of }\\eta`}

3. Sufficient statistics: a lossless summary for one model

A statistic is sufficient for a parameter when, once you know that statistic, the remaining details of the data provide no further information about that parameter under the chosen model. For independent Bernoulli trials with a shared success probability, the total number of successes is sufficient. The exact order of successes and failures does not help estimate that one probability. Sufficient does not mean useful for every question. A count of successes is sufficient for a constant Bernoulli probability, but it throws away time order, user segments, covariates, and drift—features that matter if you need a richer model.

4. Bernoulli data makes every symbol concrete

Let x be 0 or 1 and let p be its success probability. Reparameterise using the log-odds, eta = log(p / (1 - p)). Then the Bernoulli model has T(x) = x and A(eta) = log(1 + exp(eta)). Across a dataset, the sufficient statistic is just the total sum(x). {`p(x|\\eta)=\\exp\\left(x\\eta-\\log(1+e^\\eta)\\right), \\qquad p=\\frac{1}{1+e^{-\\eta}}`} {`import math observations = [1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1] successes, n = sum(observations), len(observations) p_mle = successes / n eta = math.log(p_mle / (1 - p_mle)) log_partition = math.log1p(math.exp(eta)) print(successes, n, p_mle) print(round(eta, 3), round(log_partition, 3)) print(round(n / (1 + math.exp(-eta)), 3))`} {`6 8 0.75 1.099 1.386 6.0`} The last line is the model's expected number of successes at the fitted parameter. At maximum likelihood, the expected sufficient statistic matches the observed sufficient statistic. This moment-matching view generalises across exponential families.

5. The log-partition function is doing real work

A(eta) is more than a normalising constant. Its gradient gives the expected sufficient statistic, and its Hessian gives its covariance. In the Bernoulli case, the first derivative is the sigmoid probability and the second derivative is its variance p(1 - p). This is why gradients and curvature in logistic regression have such a clean form. {`\\nabla_{\\eta}A(\\eta)=\\mathbb{E}_{\\eta}[T(X)], \\qquad \\nabla^2_{\\eta}A(\\eta)=\\operatorname{Cov}_{\\eta}[T(X)]`}

6. The connection to common ML models

A generalised linear model selects an exponential-family likelihood and relates its natural parameter to features. Logistic regression uses Bernoulli likelihood and the logit link. Multiclass logistic regression uses categorical likelihood and softmax. Poisson regression models counts with a log link. Linear regression with Gaussian noise is another member of the same broad family. The likelihood should fit the data type; do not use a sigmoid merely because a classifier tutorial did. Conjugate priors often arise naturally for exponential-family likelihoods. A Beta prior updates a Bernoulli likelihood, a Dirichlet prior updates categorical counts, and a Gamma prior updates Poisson counts. This is why the sufficient statistics from the data can produce simple posterior updates.

7. How to use this knowledge well

Start with the outcome: binary, count, continuous, categorical, or positive-valued. State the independence and variance assumptions. Identify the statistic that the likelihood treats as informative, then ask what context it discards. Use natural parameters and stable library loss functions rather than manually computing probabilities near zero or one. Finally, check calibration and residual behaviour—an elegant family cannot compensate for a mismatched data-generating process. For daily website visits modelled as Poisson, identify the sufficient statistic for a constant rate and the usual link function for a feature-based rate model. Then explain why a single total count would be insufficient if weekday seasonality matters.

import math

observations = [1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1]
successes, n = sum(observations), len(observations)
p_mle = successes / n
eta = math.log(p_mle / (1 - p_mle))
log_partition = math.log1p(math.exp(eta))

print(successes, n, p_mle)
print(round(eta, 3), round(log_partition, 3))
print(round(n / (1 + math.exp(-eta)), 3))
